title: Left alone to say "we believe"?
hookLine: do people think they will be left to say we believe and not be tested (29:2)
last: DO GOOD AS GOOD WAS DONE.

lines: A LUMP THAT LOOKS LIKE GOLD.
cards: A goldsmith has a lump of metal that looks like gold. Right color, heavy, and the customer swears it's pure. But she doesn't take anyone's word for it.
Into the crucible it goes, and up goes the heat. Whatever isn't gold separates and burns away, and what's left is what it really was all along.
Surah Al-'Ankabut, the Spider, the twenty-ninth, opens with a question a lot like that crucible.

teach.b: After the opening letters, alif, lam, mim, the surah asks. Pickthall: "Do men imagine that they will be left (at ease) because they say, We believe, and will not be tested with affliction?"

The next verse answers: those before them were tested too, so that God would make known those who are truthful and those who lie. The word for being tested comes from the root of fitnah, today's word.
In the old Arabic dictionaries, the root's first meaning is the goldsmith's: putting gold or silver into fire to separate pure from impure.

From there it spread: a trial, a temptation that pulls at you, and elsewhere turmoil and civil strife, when a whole community goes through the fire. The Qur'an even calls wealth and children a fitnah.

So the test isn't only the hard thing; it can be the good thing, and what you do with it. Tradition places this surah in Mecca, when early Muslims were being pressured, some tortured, for their faith.
The verse doesn't promise them comfort. It tells them this is what faith is like: saying we believe is the first step, and the fire shows what it's made of.
A hadith in Tirmidhi says the people most severely tested are the prophets, then those most like them, and that a person is tested according to the strength of their faith.
Read that way, a test is not a punishment and not a sign of being forgotten. In the Qur'an's picture, the crucible is a way of being taken seriously.

how: Muslims understand trials, hardships and even blessings as tests from God, and many recite 29:2–3 and ask God for steadfastness in times of difficulty.

o: a gift given as a reward for belief
a punishment for having weak faith
a trial that shows what faith is made of

games.q: faith is tested — tap the pairs.
p: a trial; gold put in the fire

s: the root of fitnah first meant refining metal in fire
the old dictionaries give it: putting gold or silver in fire to test it.
in the Qur'an, only hardships count as tests
wealth and children are also called a fitnah.
the verse promises believers an easy life
it says those before them were tested too, and so will they be.

games.q: you've said 'we believe', and now it's getting hard. what does the opening of Al-'Ankabut tell you?
o: you must have done something wrong.
being tested is what faith is like.
say it louder, and the test will stop.
games.why: 29:2–3: people won't be left just to say we believe; those before were tested too, so the truthful are made known.

practice: Run through the day ahead, or the day behind, and find one place where something pushed on what you say you believe: impatience, a corner to cut, gossip to join, a good thing that could make you proud.
Don't judge it; just see it clearly, as a goldsmith looks at what comes out of the fire, and name it: that was the test. If you pray, you can ask to be steady through it.

wordCard.voice: Fitnah. A trial: from a root meaning to put gold in the fire, then any test, temptation or turmoil that shows what faith is made of. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: fitnah, a trial or test; the root first meant refining gold in fire.

carryVoice: Your line: faith is tested. Even good things can be part of the test. Until tomorrow.
